source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, View of Lowell, Massachusetts (1840-1860), public domain
stem: The mills in the image were part of the Market Revolution. Which of the following best describes how the mills changed work?

options.text: Farm women took wage jobs tending machines, earning cash instead of making goods at home.
Enslaved workers were brought north from plantations to run the mills under overseers.
options.misconception: Lowell's mills hired free young women, not enslaved workers; slavery was a southern system.

options.text: Skilled craftsmen took over the mills and set their own prices for the cloth.
options.misconception: The mills replaced skilled craftsmen with machines tended by low-paid workers.

options.text: Farmers stopped growing crops and moved into the mills to work as owners.
options.misconception: Farmers' daughters took mill jobs, but farmers themselves kept farming; few became mill owners.

rationales.A: The Lowell mills hired young women straight off New England farms. Background: they lived in company boarding houses, tended power looms for cash wages, and sent money home.
rationales.B: Lowell's mills hired free young women, not enslaved workers. Slavery was a southern system.
rationales.C: The mills replaced skilled craftsmen with machines tended by low-paid workers.
rationales.D: Farmers' daughters took mill jobs, but farmers themselves kept farming. Few became mill owners.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the old way. A farm family made its own cloth at home, by hand.
2. Look at the new way. Machines in a big mill do the spinning and weaving, and one worker tends many machines.
3. Ask who the worker is. A young farm woman, paid in cash wages, living away from home.
4. Put it together. Work moved out of the home and into the factory, and pay became money, not goods.
Remember: the Market Revolution turned making things at home into working for wages.
